notes.18.144: 18.144 'per vaghezza' may mean 'from wandering' or 'for pleasure'. 19.4: the Greater Fortune (Fortuna Major) is a geomantic figure, likened to stars rising before dawn. 19.22 'vago' may go with Ulysses ('eager') or with his course ('wandering'). 19.31: the subject of 'prendea' is unexpressed; taken as Virgil.
notes.22.62: 22.66 ‘prima appresso Dio m’alluminasti’: taken as ‘first gave me light toward (concerning) God’; also read as ‘next after God, you first enlightened me’.
notes.2.11: 2.26 ‘mentre che’ taken in its old sense ‘until’. 2.44 ‘faria beato pur descripto’: sense disputed; also understood as ‘blessedness seemed written on him’, after a variant reading. 2.46 is Latin in the original: ‘When Israel went out of Egypt’ (Psalm 113/114).
notes.5.98: 5.112 ‘Giunse’ taken as ‘joined’ (the devil joined evil will to intellect); it can also be read ‘came’ (‘there came that evil will … with intellect’).
notes.9.74: 9.97 ‘perso’ is a dark colour, purple mixed with black; rendered ‘purple-black’.

nodes.text: now the little boat of my wit,
which leaves behind it so cruel a sea;
and I will sing of that second kingdom
where the human spirit is purged
and becomes worthy to rise to heaven.
But here let dead poetry rise again,
O holy Muses, since I am yours;
turning a little toward the other pole,
there where the Wain had already disappeared,
I saw near me an old man, alone,
worthy in his look of so much reverence
that no son owes more to a father.
A long beard, mixed with white hair,
he wore, like the hair of his head,
which fell to his chest in a double strand.
The rays of the four holy lights
so adorned his face with light
that I saw him as if the sun were before him.
“Who are you, who against the blind river
have fled the eternal prison?”
he said, moving those venerable plumes.
“Who has guided you, or what was a lamp to you
as you came out of the deep night
that keeps the valley of Hell forever black?
Are the laws of the abyss broken, then?
or has heaven changed to some new counsel,
that, though damned, you come to my rocks?”
My leader then took hold of me,
and with words and with hands and with signs
made my legs and my brow reverent.
Then he answered him: “I did not come of myself:
a lady came down from heaven, at whose prayers
I helped this man with my company.
But since it is your will that more be unfolded
of our condition, how it truly is,
my will cannot be that it be denied you.
This man has never seen his last evening;
but by his folly he was so close to it
that very little time was left to turn.
As I said, I was sent to him
to save him; and there was no other way
than this one, on which I have set out.
I have shown him all the guilty people;
and now I mean to show those spirits
who purge themselves under your charge.
How I have brought him would take long to tell you;
from on high comes down a power that helps me
lead him to see you and to hear you.
Now may it please you to welcome his coming:
he goes seeking freedom, which is so dear,
as he knows who gives up life for it.
You know it, for, for its sake, death was not bitter to you
in Utica, where you left
the garment that on the great day will shine so bright.
The eternal edicts are not broken by us,
for this man lives, and Minos does not bind me;
like people who are thinking of their road,
who move on in heart and in body remain.
And look: as, overtaken by the morning,
through the thick vapors Mars glows red
low in the west above the level of the sea,
so there appeared to me—may I see it again—
a light coming over the sea so swiftly
that no flight could equal its motion.
When I had drawn back from it a little
my eye to question my leader,
I saw it again, grown brighter and larger.
Then on each side of it there appeared to me
something white, I did not know what, and from beneath,
little by little, another came out from it.
My master still had not said a word
until the first white shapes appeared as wings;
then, when he clearly knew the boatman,
he cried: “Quick, quick, bend your knees.
Here is the angel of God: fold your hands;
from now on you will see officers like this.
See how he scorns human means,
so that he wants no oar, nor any sail other
than his wings, between shores so distant.
See how he holds them straight toward heaven,
stirring the air with the eternal feathers
that do not change like mortal hair.”
Then, as more and more toward us came
the divine bird, the brighter he appeared,
so that my eye could not bear him close at hand,
but I lowered it; and he came on to the shore
with a vessel so slender and light
that the water swallowed none of it.
At the stern stood the heavenly helmsman,
such that even described he would make [one] blessed;
and more than a hundred spirits sat inside.
“In exitu Israel de Aegypto”
they were all singing together with one voice,
with all of that psalm that is written after it.
Then he made over them the sign of the holy cross;
at which they all flung themselves onto the shore,
and he went off, as he had come, swiftly.
The crowd that remained there seemed unfamiliar
with the place, gazing around,
I arrived, pierced in the throat,
fleeing on foot and bloodying the plain.
There I lost my sight and my speech;
in the name of Mary I ended, and there
I fell, and my flesh was left alone.
I will tell the truth, and you tell it again among the living:
the angel of God took me, and the one from hell
cried out: ‘O you from heaven, why do you rob me?
You carry off with you this man’s eternal part
for one little tear that takes him from me;
but with the other part I will deal another way!’
You know well how in the air there gathers
that moist vapor which returns to water
as soon as it rises to where the cold seizes it.
He joined that evil will, which seeks only evil,
with intellect, and stirred the mist and the wind
by the power that his nature gave.
Then the valley, once the day was spent,
from Pratomagno to the great ridge, he covered
with fog; and he made the sky above so dense
that the pregnant air turned into water;
the rain fell, and to the gullies came
whatever of it the ground could not bear;
and as it gathered into the great streams,
toward the royal river so swiftly
it rushed headlong that nothing held it back.
My frozen body, at its mouth,
the raging Archiano found; and it thrust it
into the Arno, and loosened on my breast the cross
that I made of myself when the pain overcame me;
it rolled me along the banks and along the bed,
then covered and wrapped me with its spoils.”
“Ah, when you have returned to the world
and rested from the long road,”
afterwards silently look upward,
as if waiting, pale and humble;
and I saw come out from on high and descend
two angels with two flaming swords,
broken off and deprived of their points.
that there, where before it had seemed to me broken,
just like a crack that splits a wall,
I saw a gate, and three steps below
to go up to it, of different colors,
and a gatekeeper who as yet said not a word.
And as I opened my eye on it more and more,
I saw him sitting on the topmost step,
such in his face that I could not bear it;
and he had a naked sword in his hand,
which reflected the rays toward us so
that I often turned my eyes to it in vain.
“Say it from there: what do you want?”
he began to say, “where is your escort?
Take care that coming up does not harm you.”
“A lady from heaven, who knows these things,”
my master answered him, “just now
told us: ‘Go there: there is the gate.’”
“And may she further your steps in good,”
the courteous gatekeeper began again:
“Come forward, then, to our steps.”
We came there; and the first step
was white marble, so polished and clean
that I was mirrored in it just as I appear.
The second was darker in hue than purple-black,
of a rough and scorched stone,
cracked lengthwise and across.
The third, which lies massive on top,
seemed to me porphyry, as flaming
as blood that spurts out of a vein.
On this he kept both his feet,
the angel of God, sitting on the threshold,
which seemed to me a stone of diamond.
Up the three steps, with good will,
my leader drew me, saying: “Ask
humbly that he undo the lock.”
Devoutly I threw myself at the holy feet;
I asked for mercy and that he open for me,
but first I struck myself three times on the breast.
Seven P’s on my forehead he traced
with the point of the sword, and “See that you wash away,
when you are inside, these wounds,” he said.
Ashes, or earth that is dug out dry,
would be of one color with his robe;
and from beneath it he drew out two keys.
One was of gold and the other was of silver;
first with the white and then with the yellow
he so worked the gate that I was content.
“Whenever one of these keys fails,
so that it does not turn rightly in the lock,”
he said to us, “this passage does not open.
One is more precious; but the other needs a great deal
of skill and wit before it unlocks,
because it is the one that undoes the knot.
I hold them from Peter; and he told me to err
rather in opening than in keeping it locked,
provided the people throw themselves down at my feet.”

gaze at the scattered limbs of the Giants.
I saw Nimrod at the foot of the great work,
as if bewildered, and looking at the peoples
who in Shinar were proud along with him.
O Niobe, with what grieving eyes
I saw you traced upon the road,
he first let out; and then he began: “Brother,
the world is blind, and you surely come from it.
You who are living refer every cause
only up to the heavens, just as if they moved
all things along with them by necessity.
If that were so, there would be destroyed in you
free will, and it would not be justice
to have joy for good and grief for evil.
The heavens set your motions going;
I do not say all of them, but, supposing I said so,
light is given you for good and for wickedness,
and free will; which, if it endures strain
in its first battles with the heavens,
then conquers all, if it is well nourished.
To a greater power and to a better nature
you, being free, are subject; and that creates
the mind in you, which the heavens do not have in their charge.
Therefore, if the present world goes astray,
in you is the cause, in you let it be sought;
that I closed my eyes in my wandering,
and turned my thinking into dream.
At the hour when the heat of day can no longer
warm the cold of the moon,
overcome by earth, and at times by Saturn —
when the geomancers see their Greater Fortune
in the east, before the dawn,
rise by a path that stays dark for it only a little —
there came to me in a dream a stammering woman,
cross-eyed, and crooked on her feet,
with maimed hands, and sallow in colour.
I gazed at her; and as the sun revives
the cold limbs that the night weighs down,
so my look made nimble
her tongue, and then set her fully upright
in a little while, and her wan face,
just as love wants, so it coloured for her.
When she had her speech set loose in this way,
she began to sing, so that only with difficulty
could I have turned my attention away from her.
“I am,” she sang, “I am the sweet siren
who leads sailors astray in mid-sea,
so full am I of pleasure to hear!
I turned Ulysses from his wandering way
to my song; and whoever grows used to me
seldom leaves, so wholly do I content him!”
Her mouth was not yet closed again
when a lady appeared, holy and quick,
close beside me, to put that one to confusion.
“O Virgil, Virgil, who is this?”
she was saying fiercely; and he came
with his eyes fixed only on that virtuous one.
He seized the other, and laid her open in front,
tearing her clothes, and showed me her belly;
this woke me with the stench that came from it.
I moved my eyes, and the good master: “At least three
times I have called you!” he was saying. “Rise and come;
a new vision that bends me toward itself,
so that I cannot draw away from thinking of it.”
“You saw,” he said, “that ancient witch
who alone, above us, is now wept for;
you saw how a man gets free of her.
Let that be enough, and strike the ground with your heels;
turn your eyes to the lure that is whirled
by the eternal King with the great wheels.”
Like the falcon, which first looks at its feet,
then turns at the call and stretches forward
that Rome drew me, a man of Toulouse, to herself,
where I deserved to have my temples decked with myrtle.
Statius is what people back there still call me:
I sang of Thebes, and then of great Achilles;
but I fell on the way with the second burden.
The seeds of my ardor were the sparks
provided that its flame showed outwardly;
so, from the hour when there came down among us,
into the limbo of hell, Juvenal,
who made your affection known to me,
my goodwill toward you was such as
lifted your darkness so, that you then set
your sails thereafter behind the fisherman?”
And he to him: “You first sent me on the way
toward Parnassus to drink in its caves,
and you first, toward God, gave me light.
You did as one who walks by night,
who carries the light behind him and does not help himself,
but makes the people after him wise,
when you said: ‘The age is renewed;
justice returns, and the first age of humankind,
and a new progeny comes down from heaven.’
Through you I was a poet, through you a Christian:
but so that you may better see what I outline,
I will reach out my hand to color it in.
